name: glslviewer
desc: Live-coding console tool that renders GLSL Shaders
why: Live-coding GLSL shaders from the console turns a text file into moving pixels within seconds, a genuine visual payoff.

brief.what_it_is: GlslViewer is a console-based OpenGL sandbox that displays 2D and 3D GLSL fragment and vertex shaders without a UI. It takes shader source files (plus optional textures, cubemaps, and 3D models such as OBJ, PLY, LST, or GLTF) and renders them in a window, with hot reload when files change. Interaction happens through the POSIX console stdin/stdout or OSC, so you can wrap it with your own UI or a Python module. The Homebrew formula installs three executables: glslScreenSaver, glslThumbnailer, and glslViewer (the executable names come from the brew metadata, not the README).
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a flexible sandbox for displaying GLSL shaders without the need of a UI, so that other tools and UIs can drive it. The homepage invites people to join the #GlslViewer channel on the shader.zone Discord to learn how to use it, share work, and get help.
brief.how_it_works: Shaders are loaded from files and rendered in an OpenGL context, with #include dependencies resolved and automatically generated defines for platform, buffers, render passes, geometry attributes, and materials. Changes to files trigger a hot reload. Runtime control is done by sending console IN commands or OSC messages that add or delete #defines and set custom uniforms (float, int, vec2, vec3, vec4). The README does not describe the internal rendering pipeline in detail.
brief.install_notes: The README does not give install commands. It links to wiki pages titled Installing, Compile on Linux, Compile on MacOS, Compile on Windows, and Compile as WebAssembly, which suggests building from source is the documented route. I did not fetch those wiki pages. Homebrew is the user's listed install path, and the brew caveats field is empty.
brief.standout: It is a shader sandbox with no built-in UI whose main interface is plain POSIX stdin/stdout and OSC, so any script or language can drive a live shader. It also covers a wide range of inputs (video, camera, audio textures, PBR 3D models, headless rendering, PNG sequence export, a HoloPlay Looking Glass mode, and screensaver mode) in one console tool.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched homepage and README show no release date, last commit date, or deprecation note. The README still mentions Travis CI in its acknowledgements, which hints at older setup, but that is not evidence of current activity.
brief.caveats: Installing from Homebrew is the only path I checked; the wiki says compiling from source is the route on each OS, and I did not verify the build steps. The README does not state a license. The feature list is long, so some items may be unevenly maintained; I could not check that from the README. The scout note's claim that it turns a text file into moving pixels within seconds is plausible but not stated in the README. The Homebrew caveats field is empty.
